Optical flow: ṗ is the projection of Ṗ
Drag the big dot P in the figure to move the 3D point (its image p stays on the ray O→P). Drag empty space to orbit; use Reset View to return to the textbook pose.
The true tip of ṗ (Δt = 1) is marked by the small green bead on the image plane.

plan.contextChunk: This figure illustrates how the 3D motion of a point projects into 2D motion on the image plane under a pinhole camera model. A 3D point P moves through space with instantaneous velocity Ṗ, and the green line from the camera center O through P shows the projection ray, which pierces the image plane at the corresponding 2D image point p. The red arrow at P labeled Ṗ marks the point's 3D velocity, while the red arrow at p labeled ṗ marks the resulting instantaneous velocity of its 2D projection; the dashed line traces where the displaced 3D point projects, making clear that the 2D velocity is the projection of the 3D velocity rather than a simple rescaling of it. This figure motivates the perspective-projection relations x = fX/Z and y = fY/Z, and their time derivatives, as the mathematical link between a point's 3D velocity Ṗ = (Ẋ, Ẏ, Ż) in world coordinates and its observed 2D optical flow ṗ = (ẋ, ẏ) in the camera plane.

elements: Image plane drawn as a tall quadrilateral with thick dark-gray outline (no fill), seen obliquely so its far edge (toward O, screen-left) appears shorter than its near edge
Camera center O: large black filled dot at screen-left, slightly outside/behind the image plane
3D scene point P: large black filled dot far to the right, above the level of O
Green solid projection ray from O through the image plane out to P
Image point p: small black filled dot lying on the image plane exactly where the O→P ray pierces it
Red thick arrow at P representing the 3D velocity vector Ṗ, pointing up-and-back toward the camera
Red thick arrow at p (on the image plane) representing the projected 2D velocity ṗ, pointing left/up along the plane
Green dashed ray from O through the displaced image point (p + ṗ) to the displaced 3D point (P + Ṗ)
Text labels: 'O' below-left of the camera center, 'P' right of the 3D point, 'p' below the image point, 'Ṗ' above the red 3D arrow, 'ṗ' above the red 2D arrow

interactions.teaches: Moving the 3D point P shows that its image p is always the pierce point of the ray O→P: sliding P sideways sweeps p across the plane, while pushing P farther away shrinks both the image displacement and the projected velocity as 1/Z.
Rotating the scene reveals that p, P and O are truly collinear in 3D and that ṗ lies in the image plane while Ṗ does not.

interactions.label: Ẋ (lateral velocity)
interactions.teaches: Lateral 3D motion produces an image-plane flow component ẋ = f·Ẋ/Z, i.e. the same world speed yields less optical flow the farther the point is.

interactions.label: Ẏ (vertical velocity)
interactions.teaches: Vertical 3D motion maps to vertical image flow scaled by f/Z, independent of where the point sits in the image.

interactions.label: Ż (motion along optical axis)
interactions.teaches: Motion in depth creates flow that points radially away from (or toward) the principal point and vanishes at the image center — the term −(x·Ż)/Z, which is why ṗ is not merely a rescaled copy of Ṗ.

interactions.label: Advance P along Ṗ
interactions.teaches: Watching P slide along its velocity vector while p traces the corresponding path on the plane makes ṗ visibly the time derivative of the projection, not an independent quantity.

demo_steps.title: The projection ray
demo_steps.narration: With almost no motion, only the geometry remains: the green ray from camera center O through P pierces the image plane at p, the projection of P.

demo_steps.title: Pure lateral motion
demo_steps.narration: Give P a purely sideways velocity Ẋ. The red arrow at p is parallel to it and scaled by f/Z — the same world speed appears slower when the point is far away.

demo_steps.title: Pure motion in depth
demo_steps.narration: Now move P only along the optical axis. The 3D arrow points straight away from the camera, yet the image flow ṗ points radially outward from the image center — proof that ṗ is a projection, not a rescaling, of Ṗ.

demo_steps.title: General 3D velocity
demo_steps.narration: Combine all three components to reproduce the textbook figure: the dashed ray through the displaced point P+Ṗ pierces the plane at p+ṗ.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World frame = camera frame: O at origin (0,0,0); optical axis +Z runs to screen-RIGHT toward P; +Y is screen-up; +X recedes into the screen toward the upper-left (this is why the plane's left/far vertical edge draws shorter than its right/near edge). Focal length f = 2.5, so the image plane is the rectangle Z = 2.5, X ∈ [-1.7, 1.7], Y ∈ [-2.6, 2.6] (taller than wide, ratio ≈ 1.5:1, matching the source trapezoid); drawn as an unfilled quad with a thick dark-gray outline (#333333, ~4px). Default P = (X, Y, Z) = (0.35, 1.0, 9.0); dot radius ≈ 0.22. Projection: p = (f·X/Z, f·Y/Z) at Z = f, so default p ≈ (0.097, 0.278, 2.5); dot radius ≈ 0.12. Default velocity Ṗ = (Ẋ, Ẏ, Ż) = (0.2, 0.8, −2.0) — up and back toward the camera, matching the red arrow that points up-left in the source; draw it from P with Δt = 1 (arrow length ≈ |Ṗ|, shaft ~0.09 thick). Image flow from the perspective derivatives: ẋ = f(Ẋ·Z − X·Ż)/Z², ẏ = f(Ẏ·Z − Y·Ż)/Z²; draw ṗ from p in the plane with the SAME Δt = 1 so the dashed ray from O through (p+ṗ) exactly hits (P+Ṗ). Colors: rays and ray-dash #00E000 bright green (solid ray O→P, dashed ray O→P+Ṗ, dash pattern ~0.18/0.12, slightly translucent where it passes behind the plane); velocity arrows pure red #FF0000; dots and plane outline near-black #1A1A1A; labels in bold black serif, 'O' placed below-left of O, 'P' to the lower-right of P, 'p' just below p, 'Ṗ' above the midpoint of the 3D arrow, 'ṗ' above the tip of the 2D arrow. O sits slightly to the screen-left of, and outside, the image-plane quad's silhouette, exactly as in the source.
interactionPlan.notes: Use THREE.PerspectiveCamera (fov ~35) positioned so the pose matches the source trapezoid; Line2/LineMaterial (or fat-line shader) for the ~4px green and gray strokes, LineDashedMaterial equivalent for the displaced ray. Velocity arrows: custom cylinder shaft + cone head grouped so scale follows the slider values live. Render image-plane dot p and its arrow with polygonOffset / tiny Z-offset (+0.002) so they never z-fight the plane quad. Labels as CSS2DRenderer sprites that keep constant screen size and stay upright while orbiting. Drag of P via raycast onto a plane through P parallel to the screen; clamp Z to [3, 16] so p never leaves the image rectangle, and clamp X,Y so p stays inside. Recompute p, ṗ, and the dashed ray every frame from the projection formulas rather than tweening geometry. Animation advances a phase t ∈ [0,1] moving a ghost copy of P along Ṗ with its ghost image point tracing a faint trail on the plane.

authoredContext:
A 3D point will follow a trajectory $\mathbf{P}(t) = (X(t),Y(t),Z(t))$,
in camera coordinates (-optical_flow_basic_motion_point). As the
point moves, it has an instantaneous 3D velocity of
$\dot{\mathbf{P}} = (\dot{X}(t), \dot{Y}(t), \dot{Z}(t))$. The
projection of this point into the image plane location is
$\mathbf{p}(t) = (x(t),y(t))$ and its projection will move with the 2D
instantaneous velocity $\dot{\mathbf{p}} = (\dot{x}(t), \dot{y}(t))$,
where all the derivatives are done with respect to time, $t$.

A 3D point, $\mathbf{P}$, moving in the world projects a 2D moving point, $\mathbf{p}$, into the camera plane.

discrepancies: The optical-flow arrow ṗ is rendered very short and nearly vertical, whereas in the source it is a clearly visible leftward arrow of comparable prominence to the ṗ label; at default parameters it reads as a tiny red tick and loses its role as the figure's key quantity.
Labels (O, P, p, Ṗ, ṗ) are much less prominent than the heavy bold serif labels in the source; at default zoom they are small relative to the geometry and lack the source's visual hierarchy.

The dot sizes/scene scale differ: in the source O and P are large filled circles dominating the ends of the green ray and p is a clearly smaller dot; in the render all dots are small and the whole figure occupies a small fraction of the canvas.

Image-plane quad proportions and the position of the O→P ray relative to it differ somewhat (in the source the ray pierces the plane well inside a tall parallelogram whose near/far edges are strongly sheared); the generated plane is narrower and the pierce point sits closer to the left edge.
evaluation.notes: A faithful, genuinely 3D reconstruction of the perspective optical-flow figure with correct projection math and a rich set of meaningful controls (three velocity sliders, draggable P, motion animation, 4-step guided demo); main weaknesses are the visually tiny ṗ arrow and under-scaled dots/labels that weaken the at-a-glance match to the source.
action_items: Apply a visual exaggeration factor (or auto-scale) to the ṗ arrow so it stays comparable in screen length to the source's arrow, while keeping the numeric readout exact.
Increase label font sizes and give O/P/p a stronger bold serif hierarchy matching the source's heavy typography; enlarge dot radii for O and P.
Tighten the default framing (larger heightFraction / adjusted target) so the figure fills more of the canvas like the source crop.
Nudge the default Ṗ direction/magnitude so the dashed ray and red arrows visibly mirror the source's up-left configuration at load.

feedback.rationale: Concept, math, and interaction structure are correct; remaining issues are purely implementation details (arrow scaling, label typography, dot sizes, default framing) best fixed in generation.

discrepancies: The whole scene is rendered at a tiny fraction of the canvas (a few centimetres of a ~1000px-wide viewport), leaving the left two-thirds of the frame empty white — the source figure fills its frame, so the generated version reads as a miniature and loses all detail.
Labels O, P, p, Ṗ, ṗ, although specified at 40–48px bold serif, appear as near-illegible small glyphs in the render; the source's heavy, dominant typography hierarchy is lost.

The image-plane quad appears much narrower/more edge-on than in the source, where it is a large, clearly readable parallelogram that the green rays visibly pierce; the pierce point of the dashed ray on the plane is not discernible at the current framing.
The red Ṗ and ṗ arrows are barely visible at this scale — in the source they are the most visually prominent elements (thick red arrows with large heads) beside the green rays.
An extra green 'true tip' bead, ghost/trail animation objects and a numeric readout panel are added beyond the source; acceptable as teaching aids but they add clutter not present in the original.
evaluation.notes: Topology, colors and the optical-flow mathematics are correct and the interaction set (three velocity sliders, exaggeration toggle, drag-P, motion playback, 4-step guided demo) is rich and pedagogically apt, but the scene is framed far too small so the plane, red arrows and bold labels — the visual core of the source figure — are effectively illegible.

plan.contextChunk: This figure illustrates how the 3D motion of a point projects into 2D motion on the image plane under a pinhole camera model. A 3D point P moves through space with instantaneous velocity Ṗ, and the green line from the camera center O through P shows the projection ray, which pierces the image plane at the corresponding 2D image point p. The red arrow at P labeled Ṗ marks the point's 3D velocity, while the red arrow at p labeled ṗ marks the resulting instantaneous velocity of its 2D projection; the dashed line traces where the displaced 3D point projects, making clear that the 2D velocity is the projection of the 3D velocity rather than a simple rescaling of it. This figure motivates the perspective-projection relations x = fX/Z and y = fY/Z, and their time derivatives, as the mathematical link between a point's 3D velocity Ṗ = (Ẋ, Ẏ, Ż) in world coordinates and its observed 2D optical flow ṗ = (ẋ, ẏ) in the camera plane.

elements: Image plane drawn as a tall quadrilateral with thick dark-gray outline (no fill), seen obliquely so its far edge (toward O, screen-left) appears shorter than its near edge
Camera center O: large black filled dot at screen-left, slightly outside/behind the image plane
3D scene point P: large black filled dot far to the right, above the level of O
Green solid projection ray from O through the image plane out to P
Image point p: small black filled dot lying on the image plane exactly where the O→P ray pierces it
Red thick arrow at P representing the 3D velocity vector Ṗ, pointing up-and-back toward the camera
Red thick arrow at p (on the image plane) representing the projected 2D velocity ṗ, pointing left/up along the plane
Green dashed ray from O through the displaced image point (p + ṗ) to the displaced 3D point (P + Ṗ)
Text labels: 'O' below-left of the camera center, 'P' right of the 3D point, 'p' below the image point, 'Ṗ' above the red 3D arrow, 'ṗ' above the red 2D arrow

interactions.teaches: Moving the 3D point P shows that its image p is always the pierce point of the ray O→P: sliding P sideways sweeps p across the plane, while pushing P farther away shrinks both the image displacement and the projected velocity as 1/Z.
Rotating the scene reveals that p, P and O are truly collinear in 3D and that ṗ lies in the image plane while Ṗ does not.

interactions.label: Ẋ (lateral velocity)
interactions.teaches: Lateral 3D motion produces an image-plane flow component ẋ = f·Ẋ/Z, i.e. the same world speed yields less optical flow the farther the point is.

interactions.label: Ẏ (vertical velocity)
interactions.teaches: Vertical 3D motion maps to vertical image flow scaled by f/Z, independent of where the point sits in the image.

interactions.label: Ż (motion along optical axis)
interactions.teaches: Motion in depth creates flow that points radially away from (or toward) the principal point and vanishes at the image center — the term −(x·Ż)/Z, which is why ṗ is not merely a rescaled copy of Ṗ.

interactions.label: Advance P along Ṗ
interactions.teaches: Watching P slide along its velocity vector while p traces the corresponding path on the plane makes ṗ visibly the time derivative of the projection, not an independent quantity.

demo_steps.title: The projection ray
demo_steps.narration: With almost no motion, only the geometry remains: the green ray from camera center O through P pierces the image plane at p, the projection of P.

demo_steps.title: Pure lateral motion
demo_steps.narration: Give P a purely sideways velocity Ẋ. The red arrow at p is parallel to it and scaled by f/Z — the same world speed appears slower when the point is far away.

demo_steps.title: Pure motion in depth
demo_steps.narration: Now move P only along the optical axis. The 3D arrow points straight away from the camera, yet the image flow ṗ points radially outward from the image center — proof that ṗ is a projection, not a rescaling, of Ṗ.

demo_steps.title: General 3D velocity
demo_steps.narration: Combine all three components to reproduce the textbook figure: the dashed ray through the displaced point P+Ṗ pierces the plane at p+ṗ.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: World frame = camera frame: O at origin (0,0,0); optical axis +Z runs to screen-RIGHT toward P; +Y is screen-up; +X recedes into the screen toward the upper-left (this is why the plane's left/far vertical edge draws shorter than its right/near edge). Focal length f = 2.5, so the image plane is the rectangle Z = 2.5, X ∈ [-1.7, 1.7], Y ∈ [-2.6, 2.6] (taller than wide, ratio ≈ 1.5:1, matching the source trapezoid); drawn as an unfilled quad with a thick dark-gray outline (#333333, ~4px). Default P = (X, Y, Z) = (0.35, 1.0, 9.0); dot radius ≈ 0.22. Projection: p = (f·X/Z, f·Y/Z) at Z = f, so default p ≈ (0.097, 0.278, 2.5); dot radius ≈ 0.12. Default velocity Ṗ = (Ẋ, Ẏ, Ż) = (0.2, 0.8, −2.0) — up and back toward the camera, matching the red arrow that points up-left in the source; draw it from P with Δt = 1 (arrow length ≈ |Ṗ|, shaft ~0.09 thick). Image flow from the perspective derivatives: ẋ = f(Ẋ·Z − X·Ż)/Z², ẏ = f(Ẏ·Z − Y·Ż)/Z²; draw ṗ from p in the plane with the SAME Δt = 1 so the dashed ray from O through (p+ṗ) exactly hits (P+Ṗ). Colors: rays and ray-dash #00E000 bright green (solid ray O→P, dashed ray O→P+Ṗ, dash pattern ~0.18/0.12, slightly translucent where it passes behind the plane); velocity arrows pure red #FF0000; dots and plane outline near-black #1A1A1A; labels in bold black serif, 'O' placed below-left of O, 'P' to the lower-right of P, 'p' just below p, 'Ṗ' above the midpoint of the 3D arrow, 'ṗ' above the tip of the 2D arrow. O sits slightly to the screen-left of, and outside, the image-plane quad's silhouette, exactly as in the source.
interactionPlan.notes: Use THREE.PerspectiveCamera (fov ~35) positioned so the pose matches the source trapezoid; Line2/LineMaterial (or fat-line shader) for the ~4px green and gray strokes, LineDashedMaterial equivalent for the displaced ray. Velocity arrows: custom cylinder shaft + cone head grouped so scale follows the slider values live. Render image-plane dot p and its arrow with polygonOffset / tiny Z-offset (+0.002) so they never z-fight the plane quad. Labels as CSS2DRenderer sprites that keep constant screen size and stay upright while orbiting. Drag of P via raycast onto a plane through P parallel to the screen; clamp Z to [3, 16] so p never leaves the image rectangle, and clamp X,Y so p stays inside. Recompute p, ṗ, and the dashed ray every frame from the projection formulas rather than tweening geometry. Animation advances a phase t ∈ [0,1] moving a ghost copy of P along Ṗ with its ghost image point tracing a faint trail on the plane.

Optical flow: ṗ is the projection of Ṗ
Drag the big dot P in the figure to move the 3D point (its image p stays on the ray O→P). Drag empty space to orbit; use Reset View to return to the textbook pose.
The true tip of ṗ (Δt = 1) is marked by the small green bead on the image plane.
Guided demo
⚠ Figure failed to load

discrepancies: The image plane is rendered much narrower/taller than the source's wide oblique parallelogram; in the source the plane's near vertical edge sits well right of O and the quad reads as a large window, whereas here it is a thin slab that the ray barely crosses.
The Ṗ arrow is drawn much shorter than in the source (almost all head, little shaft), so the visual link between P + Ṗ and the dashed ray endpoint is weaker than the long red vector in the original.

The default ṗ arrow points nearly straight up, while the source shows it pointing left-ish roughly along the dashed pierce direction; the default Ẋ/Ẏ/Ż preset gives a different in-plane flow orientation than the textbook pose.
Extra elements not in the source: a light grey plane fill, a green 'true tip' bead, and a '×4.2' exaggeration annotation beside the ṗ label (pedagogically justified but visually additive).

O in the source sits clearly outside/left of the plane with the solid green ray visibly crossing the plane boundary near its lower-left corner; in the render the crossing geometry is compressed and less legible.
evaluation.notes: A faithful and conceptually correct optical-flow figure with the right primitives (plane quad, O/P/p dots, green solid and dashed rays, red Ṗ and ṗ arrows) and an unusually rich, well-targeted interaction set; the main shortfalls are proportion — a too-narrow image plane and a stubby Ṗ arrow — plus a default flow direction that differs from the textbook pose.
action_items: Widen the image plane quad (increase half-width relative to height) and reposition it so the oblique parallelogram silhouette and the ray's pierce point read like the source.
Lengthen the Ṗ arrow shaft (or scale Δt) so the red vector spans a substantial fraction of the P-to-dashed-ray gap as in the original, with a proportionally smaller head.
Tune the default Ẋ/Ẏ/Ż preset so ṗ points left-and-slightly-up in the image plane, matching the source's arrow orientation.
Reduce visual clutter of the added bead/plane fill/'×4.2' tag in the default state (e.g., start with exaggeration off or fade the fill) so the first view matches the clean line-art of the source.
